# Bodhirājakumāra Sutta (MN 85 (PTS MN ii 91))

**ID:** MN 85 (PTS MN ii 91)

**Title (English, from literature):** With Prince Bodhi

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bodhirājakumāra Sutta* (MN 85) is the 85th discourse of the *Majjhimanikāya*, situated in the middle of the second set of fifty suttas (*Majjhimapaṇṇāsa*) [Gethin 2008]. Set in the Bhagga country at Sumsumāragiri, the dialogue takes place after Prince Bodhi (son of King Udena of Kosambī) invites the Buddha to his newly built Kokanada palace [Hazra 1982; Martin 2006]. In response to the prince's assertion that pleasure or happiness is to be attained only through hardship and pain, the Buddha recounts his own quest prior to awakening, showing the fallacy of that view [SuttaCentral; Hazra 1982; Bronkhorst 1993; Anālayo 2017]. The sutta also sets forth the "five factors of striving" (*pañca padhāniyaṅgāni*)—faith, health, honesty, energy, and wisdom—explaining how a monk endowed with these head-and-heart qualities may attain arahantship swiftly under the Teacher's guidance [Hazra 1982; Wen].

The autobiographical core of the sutta presents an extended first-person narrative combining the bodhisatta's training under his first two teachers, his practice of painful austerities, the realization of the four jhānas and three knowledges (*tevijjā*), and his earliest post-awakening encounters, culminating in the instruction to the group of five monks [Hazra 1982; Gaffney 2003; Gethin 2008; Polak 2011]. Because it shares verbatim large blocks of material found across several early discourses, modern translations and the Pali Text Society edition often abridged it via cross-references to the *Mahāsaccaka Sutta* (MN 36) and *Ariyapariyesana Sutta* (MN 26) [Gaffney 2003; Gethin 2008]. Modern scholars have discussed the text's composition in relation to these parallel biographical narratives, noting dialectal archaisms such as the optative form *huveyya* [Polak 2011; Wynne 2007]. In post-canonical literature, the story of Prince Bodhi's invitation is echoed in the Vinaya (*Cullavagga* / *Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka*, Kd 15) and the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [Burlingame 1921].

Cross-tradition parallels include a Sanskrit fragment of a *Bodharājakumārasūtra* recovered from Eastern Turkestan, as well as multiple Sanskrit and Chinese parallels in the Āgamas (e.g., MĀ 204, EĀ 31.8) and Vinaya literatures (such as the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and the *Mahāvastu*) [SuttaCentral; Martin 2006; Anālayo 2017]. DharmaNexus aligns extensive passages of MN 85 with MN 36 (over 99,000 shared characters, spanning §11.1–20.7), MN 100 (§11.1–28.2), and MN 26 (§43.2–51.16), as well as the Vinaya *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1) and Sanskrit narrative corpora including the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, the *Mahāvastu*, and the *Lalitavistara* [DharmaNexus].
